definition: The Halcyon is a home video game console produced by RDI Video Systems.
details: The system was planned to be released in January 1985, with the initial retail price for the system being US$2,500 (equivalent to $7,484 in 2025). Fewer than a dozen units are known to exist and it never reached most retailers because of a lack of affordable disc players. The design featured a LaserDisc player and an attached computer, each the size of an early-model VCR. Of the six games planned, only two games were released: Thayer's Quest and NFL Football LA Raiders vs SD Chargers. RDI Video Systems claimed that the system would be entirely voice-activated, and would have an artificial intelligence akin to HAL 9000 from 2001: A Space Odyssey.

explainer.lead: The Halcyon was an ambitious home console from RDI Video Systems that combined a LaserDisc player with an attached computer and promised entirely voice-activated control. Planned for January 1985 at US$2,500, it never reached most retailers because affordable disc players were unavailable, and fewer than a dozen units are known to exist.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a game machine that plays movies from a big shiny disc and is supposed to listen when you talk, instead of needing ordinary controls. The Halcyon tried to do that in 1985, but it was extremely expensive and its disc equipment was hard to afford. Only two games came out, and very few machines still exist.
tiers.practitioner: Treat the Halcyon as historical hardware rather than a current speech-recognition stack: its design paired a LaserDisc player with an attached computer, each roughly the size of an early VCR. Its main pitfalls were hardware affordability, failed retail distribution, and the gap between broad voice-control and AI claims and a library of only two released games.
tiers.paperLevel: Halcyon = LaserDisc player + attached computer, with entirely voice-activated operation and HAL 9000-like artificial intelligence claimed by RDI Video Systems. It was planned for January 1985 at US$2,500, equivalent to $7,484 in 2025. Its known limits were dependence on unaffordable disc players, negligible retail availability, fewer than a dozen surviving known units, and only two released games.

explainer.example: A Halcyon owner could play Thayer's Quest, one of the console's two released games. The other was NFL Football LA Raiders vs SD Chargers; the remaining four planned games were not released.

explainer.intuition: The Halcyon tried to make a home console feel like an intelligent machine you could operate by speaking. Its LaserDisc player supplied the disc-based gaming side, while an attached computer formed the other half of the unusually large system.
howItWorks: The design combined a LaserDisc player and an attached computer.
Each component was about the size of an early-model VCR.
RDI Video Systems said operation would be entirely voice-activated.
The company also claimed an artificial intelligence akin to HAL 9000.
Players could run one of the two titles that actually reached release.
explainer.whyItMatters: The Halcyon shows that voice control and AI-like interaction were being promoted in home entertainment as early as its planned 1985 launch. It also illustrates how hardware cost and availability can stop an ambitious system before it reaches ordinary shops.
misconceptions: It was not a widely available retail console: it never reached most retailers.
It did not receive all six planned games; only two were released.
The voice activation and HAL-like intelligence were claims made by RDI Video Systems.
